The first challenges for neonate Mohave ground squirrels (Xerospermophilus mohavensis, family Sciuridae) are substantial, as newborns emerge remarkably altricial, with a wet weight at birth of only 4.5 grams [Wwb = 4.5 grams]. Survival during this early stage depends critically on the mother's ability to provide both warmth and nutrition within the subterranean burrow, where conditions remain relatively stable. The onset of lactation soon after parturition provides the concentrated milk necessary for the pup's rapid growth, yet the total period of dependence is brief. Weaning occurs at 36 days after birth [tx = 36 days after birth], a remarkably short interval for a sciurid of this size when assessed at a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. At the point of weaning, the juvenile has achieved a wet weight at weaning of 30 grams [Wwx = 30 grams], representing a more than six-fold increase from the neonate's mass. This phase of pre-weaning development is energetically demanding on the lactating female, who must forage extensively during her active above-ground periods to compensate for the rapid nutrient transfer to her litter.

Females of this species typically bear a single annual litter, producing up to 6 pups per litter [N_R_i = up to 6 pups per litter]. Given that only one reproductive event occurs each year [F_R_i = one reproductive event occurs each year], this yields a modest annual reproductive output that aligns with the strategy of a relatively long-lived species inhabiting an arid environment with unpredictable resource pulses. At a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the total gestation period during which the embryos develop in utero is 24 days [tg = 24 days]. This brief gestation, combined with the even shorter lactation period, suggests that the reproductive cycle is tightly compressed into the narrow window of spring green-up and moderate temperatures characteristic of the Mojave Desert. Following weaning, the juvenile enters a sub-adult phase of continued somatic growth before reaching the threshold for reproductive competence. Puberty in this species occurs at 300 days after birth [tp = 300 days after birth], indicating that a young squirrel born in the spring will not become reproductively active until the subsequent breeding season, a full annual cycle later at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C].

The progression of juvenile development culminates in the attainment of the species' ultimate wet weight, recorded at approximately 150 grams [Wwi = approximately 150 grams] for fully grown adults. This adult mass is modest compared to many other ground-dwelling sciurids, reflecting an adaptation to the energetic constraints of a desert existence where thermoregulation and water conservation impose significant costs. The transition from the neonatal mass of 4.5 grams [Wwb = 4.5 grams] at birth to this adult asymptote requires a substantial investment in foraging and nutrient assimilation, particularly during the brief periods of peak resource availability following winter rains. The sub-adult growth phase is characterized by a steady accumulation of body reserves, as the young animal must build the lipid stores necessary to survive its first hibernation period. This mass gain is most rapid in the weeks immediately following weaning at 30 grams [Wwx = 30 grams], when the juvenile begins to exploit the same seed and herbaceous resources as the adults. The efficiency of this growth trajectory is strongly modulated by the timing of spring emergence, with early-born individuals often reaching a larger pre-hibernation mass than their later-born counterparts.

Longevity records for this species remain somewhat uncertain due to the difficulty of mark-recapture studies in harsh desert terrain, but available data indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 7.8 years [am = approximately 7.8 years] when maintained at a typical body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This places the Mohave ground squirrel among the longer-lived small mammals relative to its body size, a life-history pattern consistent with its low annual fecundity and the high risks of mortality associated with its extreme environment. The reproductive strategy is thus one of iteroparity, where each female has multiple opportunities across several years to produce offspring. The onset of puberty at 300 days after birth [tp = 300 days after birth] means that a young female who survives her first hibernation can contribute to the next generation, though her early reproductive attempts may be constrained by her smaller body mass and inexperience at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. As the animal ages, physiological decline and tooth wear ultimately lead to senescence and an age-related death, with very few individuals reaching the upper boundary of the known lifespan.

When assessed at the typical euthermic core temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the species exhibits a maximum reproductive rate of 6 pups per year [Ri = 6 pups per year], a modest output that reflects the tight coupling of reproduction to the brief spring growing season. This aggregate rate, derived from a single litter of 6 pups per litter [N_R_i = 6 pups per litter] produced just once each year [F_R_i = once each year], is considerably lower than that of many temperate-zone squirrels that can produce multiple litters. The environmental constraints of the Mojave Desert are severe; summer temperatures can exceed 40 °C for weeks on end, forcing the animals into obligate estivation during the hottest months. This extended period of torpor effectively truncates the active season available for foraging, growth, and offspring rearing. The coordination of all life-history events, from weaning at 36 days after birth [tx = 36 days after birth] to the accumulation of pre-hibernation fat reserves, must therefore be precisely timed to avoid the lethal combination of heat, desiccation, and food scarcity that characterizes the desert summer at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C].
